name: Pinking craft scissors
description: Light craft scissors with zigzag blades and bright plastic loops. They leave a decorative edge on paper and cloth, but they are poor at anything tougher.
notes: Laid flat and opened a little, 156 mm long: two 92 mm stainless blades with a row of teeth on each cutting edge, a pivot screw and orange finger loops. Mass matches the reference. The reference's negative butchering quality has no counterpart here; leaving butchering out keeps them off that job.

name: Stapler
description: A desk stapler with a black plastic cap over an aluminium staple channel, for pinning sheets of paper together.
notes: 160 by 38 mm and 55 mm tall, closed: rubber foot, plastic base, steel anvil at the front, aluminium magazine hinged at the back under a sloped cap. Mass matches the reference. No quality: the reference gives none, and stapling paper has no recipe use yet.

name: Bone billet
description: A thick length of leg bone, knuckled at both ends. Struck against the edge of a flint core, it knocks off thin flakes without shattering the stone.
notes: 204 mm long, 30 mm across the shaft and 44 mm at the knuckled ends, with a scuffed striking patch near one end. CHECK VOLUME (x3.95): the knobbed ends fill the bounding box's corners poorly; the bone itself is near the reference's 100 mL. Mass matches the reference. knapping is a new quality name: a soft hammer for flint knapping, distinct from hammering.

name: Wooden billet
description: A short, heavy baton of hardwood with the bark left on the grip. Used as a soft hammer to strike flakes off stone without crushing the edge.
notes: 200 mm long and 40 mm thick: oak, bark on the grip half, the striking end rounded and darkened. CHECK VOLUME (x3.2): a round baton fills its square box poorly and a 40 mm baton is chunkier than the reference's 100 mL; it reads better as a billet at play distance. Mass matches the reference. knapping is shared with the bone billet.

name: Stick rock drill
description: A straight wooden spindle with a flat, worn end. Spun against stone with wet sand under it, it slowly grinds a rough hole.
notes: 200 mm long and 30 mm thick: birch, a turned neck wrapped with cord near the top for a bow string or the palm, and a working end caked with grey grit. CHECK VOLUME (x2.05): round section in a square box. Mass matches the reference. mining 1 is the lowest grade of the rock-breaking quality, kept apart from drilling because it needs water and sand and takes much longer; that cost needs a recipe field that does not exist yet.

name: Bone punch
description: A stubby piece of bone, knuckled at one end and ground to a short point at the other. Set on a stone's edge and struck, or pressed hard, it takes off small precise flakes.
notes: 152 mm long, 36 mm across the knuckle, tapering to a short polished tip. CHECK VOLUME (x1.97): round section and knuckle in a square box. Mass matches the reference. punching is the quality name the dental tools use; here it is the punch for indirect percussion and pressure flaking.

name: Nail punch
description: A steel nail clamped between two split pieces of wood and bound tight with cord, its point standing out of one end. A harder, finer punch for flaking stone.
notes: 150 mm long and 24 mm square: two pine cheeks with a visible gap where the nail lies between them, three jute wraps, and 20 mm of nail proud at the tip. Mass matches the reference. punching 1, the nail punch grade; steel awls and leather punches are 2.

name: Bone awl
description: A sharpened sliver of bone with a knuckled grip, for piercing leather before it is stitched. It will serve as a stabbing tool in a pinch, but not for long.
notes: 150 mm long: a 75 mm bone grip with a knuckle at the end and a 75 mm spike tapering to a needle point, the spike in a paler bone finish. The reference gives no longest side; 150 mm is a judgement. Mass matches the reference. punching is the quality name for awls and punches. Its improvised stabbing attack needs melee fields left for the framework refactor.

name: Steel awl
description: A sewing awl with a turned wooden handle and a fine steel spike, for punching stitch holes through leather and canvas.
notes: Shares the bone awl's model with a walnut grip and a steel spike, carrying the reference's own 50 g. A real steel awl has a slimmer, straighter handle than the knuckled bone grip; at play distance the shared shape reads as an awl.
